summary: Michigan's knowledge test includes a road sign test, and the fastest way to read a sign is by its shape and color. The handbook lists nine basic shapes. Some shapes belong to only one sign, so you can recognize them by shape alone.

Regulatory signs tell you about specific laws that control the speed and movement of traffic. They are usually rectangles in white and black, red and white, or red, white, and black. Red on a sign means stop, prohibited, or forbidden, so a red circle with a slash over a symbol tells you that the action shown is not allowed.

At a STOP sign you must stop completely every time, at the stop line or crosswalk, or where you can see cross traffic without pulling into the intersection. At a YIELD sign you slow down, check traffic, and stop only if needed. DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY signs keep drivers from going up freeway exit ramps against traffic.

concepts.definition: The eight-sided sign is used only for STOP. Come to a complete stop and check for traffic before going on, even when no one else is in sight.
concepts.tip: Eight sides: stop all the way, every time.

concepts.definition: The triangle with its point down is used only for YIELD. Slow down, check for traffic, and be prepared to stop. Let vehicles crossing your path go first.
concepts.tip: Point down: let the other traffic go first.

concepts.definition: Regulatory signs state laws such as speed limits, turn limits, and one-way traffic. They are usually rectangular, in white and black, red and white, or red, white, and black.
concepts.tip: White rectangle: a rule, not advice.

concepts.definition: Red means stop, prohibited, or forbidden. A red circle and slash over a symbol, such as a U-turn arrow or a truck, means that action is not allowed there.
concepts.tip: Slash through it: do not do it.

concepts.term: DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY
concepts.definition: DO NOT ENTER means you may not drive in. WRONG WAY means you are already against traffic and must get out safely and quickly. Both are posted near freeway ramps.
concepts.tip: See either one: you are on the wrong ramp or road.

concepts.definition: Stop at the stop line or crosswalk. If there is neither, stop where you can see approaching traffic without pulling into the intersection.
concepts.tip: Line, then crosswalk, then where you can see.

concepts.definition: Drive at a careful and prudent speed so you can stop within the clear distance ahead. That speed is never faster than the posted limit and may be slower in bad conditions.
concepts.tip: The posted number is a ceiling, not a target.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

points: The octagon is used only for STOP, and the point-down triangle only for YIELD.
Regulatory signs are usually rectangles in black, white, and red.
A red circle and slash means the action shown is not allowed.
NO TURN ON RED means wait for the green light before turning.
If you miss a freeway exit, go to the next one; never use the median crossover.

compare.title: STOP sign or YIELD sign
rows: Full stop every time, then go when the way is clear
Red and white triangle, point down
Slow down, let others go first, stop only if needed

figures.alt: Nine labeled shapes: red octagon reading STOP, point-down triangle reading YIELD, yellow diamond (warning), yellow-green pentagon (school), yellow pennant (no passing), green wide rectangle (directions), white tall rectangle (rules), round yellow railroad sign, and white crossbuck.
figures.caption: Each shape tells you what kind of message a sign carries before you can read it.

source.title: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), FHWA
source.license: U.S. federal government work, public domain

summary: Warning signs tell you about a hazard or a change in the road ahead. Most are yellow diamonds with black letters or symbols, because the diamond shape means warning and yellow means caution. Other colors add detail: orange is for construction and maintenance, fluorescent yellow-green is for schools, pedestrians, and bicycles, and fluorescent pink marks an incident or emergency.

Railroad crossings have their own signs. The round yellow advance warning sign tells you a crossing is ahead, and the white crossbuck stands at the tracks. If a train is coming, stop between the distances given below, because trains overhang the rails. A crossing with a STOP sign requires a stop even when no train is in sight.

Work zones are marked with orange signs and may lower the speed limit while workers are present. Fines for moving violations are doubled there and speeding adds more points. Construction workers may direct traffic, and you must follow them even when a signal says otherwise. The pentagon marks a school area, and the yellow pennant on the left side of the road warns of a no-passing zone.

concepts.definition: Usually a yellow diamond with black letters or symbols. It warns of a hazard or change ahead, such as a curve, a merge, a lane ending, or a deer crossing.
concepts.tip: Diamond means: something is coming up, be ready.

concepts.definition: The round yellow sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead. If a train is coming, stop no more than 50 feet and no less than 15 feet from the tracks.
concepts.tip: Round sign: slow down, look and listen for trains.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: The white X-shaped sign that marks the railroad crossing itself. At passive crossings it may come with a YIELD or STOP sign, and there are no lights or gates.
concepts.tip: Crossbuck at the tracks; round sign before them.

concepts.definition: Orange diamond signs mark construction and maintenance areas. The speed limit is often 45 mph when workers are present, and fines for moving violations are doubled.
concepts.tip: Orange: slow down and watch for workers.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: The five-sided fluorescent yellow-green sign marks a school area or crossing. Drive carefully, watch for children, and obey a school crossing guard.
concepts.tip: Five sides: think school children.

concepts.definition: A yellow pennant-shaped sign placed on the left side of the road. It warns that conditions make passing hazardous.
concepts.tip: The pennant faces the passing lane side.

concepts.definition: An orange triangle on the back of vehicles that cannot go faster than 25 mph, such as farm machinery and horse-drawn buggies.
concepts.tip: Orange triangle: expect a very slow vehicle.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

points: Most warning signs are yellow diamonds; orange ones mark work zones.
Yellow-green is for school, pedestrian, and bicycle cautions; pink is for incidents.
When a train is coming, stop 15 to 50 feet from the tracks.
Always stop at a crossing with a STOP sign, even if no train is in sight.
Follow a construction worker's directions even if the signal says otherwise.
When your lane ends, merge and yield to traffic in the other lane.

figures.alt: Six labeled warning shapes: a yellow diamond for general warning, an orange diamond for construction, a yellow-green pentagon for school, pedestrian, and bicycle, a pink diamond for incidents, a round yellow sign with an X (railroad ahead), and an orange triangle with red border (slow vehicle).
figures.caption: The color of a warning sign tells you what kind of hazard to expect.

source.title: Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), FHWA
source.license: U.S. federal government work, public domain

summary: Guide signs help you find your way and the services you need. Their color tells you what kind of information they carry: green for directions and guidance, blue for services and hospitality, and brown for recreation and cultural places such as parks.

Route markers identify federal, state, and county roads. There are separate markers for Interstate freeways, U.S. highways, Michigan state highways, and county roads. Michigan state highways carry the letter M, as in M-32.

On freeways, exit signs show which lane to use when leaving. Slow down only after you are fully in the deceleration lane, and obey the posted exit ramp speed because many ramps curve sharply. If you miss an exit, drive to the next one; never back up or use a median crossover.

concepts.definition: Give directions and guidance, such as the way to towns, freeway exits, and distances.
concepts.tip: Green: go this way.

concepts.definition: Show services and hospitality, such as gas stations, food, lodging, and rest areas with restrooms.
concepts.tip: Blue: services for travelers.

concepts.definition: Point to places of recreation or cultural interest, such as a national park or historic site.
concepts.tip: Brown: parks and points of interest.

concepts.definition: Signs that identify the road system: Interstate freeway, U.S. highway, Michigan state highway (such as M-32), and county route.
concepts.tip: M plus a number means a Michigan state highway.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: A blue sign at a railroad crossing with a phone number and crossing ID. Use it to report a stalled vehicle on the tracks or a warning device that is not working.
concepts.tip: Stuck on the tracks with no train coming: get everyone out, then call this number.

concepts.definition: During posted peak hours, only vehicles with two or more occupants may use it. Motorcycles may use it at any time, and all drivers may use it outside the posted hours.
concepts.tip: Two or more people inside during HOV hours.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

points: Green means directions, blue means services, brown means recreation.
Route markers exist for federal, state, and county roads.
Slow down for an exit only after you are in the deceleration lane.
Obey the exit ramp speed; many ramps have sharp curves.
Missed your exit? Go on to the next exit and come back.

summary: In Michigan the red light is at the top of a traffic signal. A steady yellow light means red is coming and you must stop if you can do so safely. A flashing red light works like a STOP sign, and a flashing yellow light means go ahead carefully. If a signal is not working, stop completely and yield to vehicles already at the intersection.

Left turns are often controlled by arrows. A steady green arrow gives a protected turn because oncoming traffic is stopped. A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and people crossing. A solid yellow arrow warns that the turn signal is about to turn red.

Pavement markings are white or yellow. White lines separate lanes going the same way and mark the right edge of the road, while yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. You may pass across a broken yellow line when it is safe, but not across a solid yellow line on your side. A center lane marked with solid and broken yellow lines is only for left turns.

A Michigan Left replaces the normal left turn at some divided highways. Instead of turning left at the intersection, you go straight through and turn left into a median crossover, or turn right and then make a U-turn at a crossover.

concepts.definition: Come to a full stop, then go when the road is clear, just as at a STOP sign.
concepts.tip: Flashing red = STOP sign.

concepts.definition: Proceed carefully through the intersection, scanning traffic in both directions.
concepts.tip: Flashing yellow = slow down and look.

concepts.definition: You may turn left only after yielding to oncoming traffic, which has a green light, and to pedestrians and bicyclists.
concepts.tip: Flashing yellow arrow: your turn is not protected.

concepts.definition: Oncoming traffic is stopped, so the turn is protected. Go in the arrow's direction, but still yield to pedestrians.
concepts.tip: Green arrow: protected, but watch the crosswalk.

concepts.definition: Yellow lines separate opposite directions; white lines separate lanes going the same way and mark the right road edge. Do not cross a solid yellow line on your side to pass.
concepts.tip: Yellow = opposite ways. White = same way.

concepts.definition: Marked by a solid yellow line on each outer edge and broken yellow lines inside. Used only for left turns from either direction; passing or merging in it is illegal.
concepts.tip: Middle lane with solid and broken yellow: turn only.

concepts.definition: An indirect left turn. Drive straight past the intersection and turn left into the median crossover, or turn right first and then U-turn at a crossover.
concepts.tip: Go past, turn around in the median, come back.

points: The red light is at the top of the signal.
On steady yellow, stop if you can do it safely; never speed up.
A flashing yellow arrow means yield before turning left.
A solid yellow line on your side means no passing.
A double solid white line means same direction, but do not cross.
Bicycle lanes may not be used for driving, passing, right turns, or parking.

compare.title: Left-turn arrows
rows: Turn with caution; yield to pedestrians
Oncoming traffic has a green light
Yield, then turn when there is a safe gap
The arrow is about to turn red
Stop if approaching; finish if already in and clear
Stop; wait until the signal changes

figures.alt: Two road diagrams. Top: a two-way road with a broken yellow center line, plus a solid yellow line next to the lower lane on the right half. Bottom: two lanes going the same way, separated by a broken white line, with a solid yellow left edge and a solid white right edge.
figures.caption: Yellow lines divide opposite directions; white lines divide lanes going the same way.

summary: Right of way rules decide who goes first. Drivers turning left yield to oncoming traffic, and drivers turning right yield too, including on a red light. At a four-way stop, the first vehicle to stop goes first; if two arrive together, the vehicle on the left yields to the one on its right. At a T-intersection, traffic on the through road goes first.

Pedestrians in a crosswalk have the right of way even when your light is green. Yield to a person with a white cane or guide dog, to people crossing from a driveway or alley, and to anyone who started across before the signal changed. In a roundabout, entering traffic yields to vehicles already circling, which come from the left.

Emergency vehicles and school buses need special care. Pull to the right edge and stop for an approaching emergency vehicle with lights and siren. Slow down and move over for one that is stopped. Stop well back from a school bus with flashing red lights unless it is on the other side of a divided highway.

At railroad crossings, stop for flashing lights, bells, or lowered gates, and never go around them. Do not start across unless there is room to clear the tracks. If your car stalls on the tracks, get everyone out and away first.

concepts.definition: Stop at least 20 feet from a school bus with flashing red overhead lights, and stay stopped until the lights go off or the bus moves. Flashing yellow overhead lights mean be prepared to stop.
concepts.tip: Red lights on the bus: stop 20 feet back.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: If a barrier such as a concrete or grass median separates you from a stopped school bus on the other side, you do not have to stop. Drivers on the bus's side of the road must stop.
concepts.tip: Median between you and the bus: no stop needed.

concepts.definition: Pull to the right edge, clear of intersections, and stop for lights and siren. Stay at least 500 feet behind a moving one. For a stopped one, slow at least 10 mph below the limit and move over if safe.
concepts.tip: Moving: pull right. Stopped: slow down and move over.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: The first vehicle to stop goes first. If two arrive at the same time, the vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle on its right.
concepts.tip: Tie at a four-way stop: yield to the right.

concepts.definition: Traffic goes counterclockwise. Entering traffic yields to traffic from the left, including bicyclists and pedestrians. If an emergency vehicle comes, leave at the nearest exit and pull over.
concepts.tip: Look left, wait for a gap, never turn left to enter.

concepts.definition: Stop when lights flash, bells ring, or gates are down or moving. Do not cross unless your vehicle can clear the far side by at least 6 feet.
concepts.tip: Never stop on the tracks.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: If gates or lights activate or a train is coming, you have about 20 seconds: get everyone out and away, then call 911. If not activated, get out and call the number on the blue sign.
concepts.tip: People first, car last.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

points: Left-turning drivers yield to oncoming traffic, even on green.
Yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk even when your light is green.
Stop at least 20 feet from a school bus with flashing red lights.
Stay at least 500 feet behind a moving emergency vehicle.
Funeral processions have the right of way except over fire, ambulance, and police.
School buses, for-hire passenger vehicles, and hazmat vehicles must stop at railroad crossings unless the crossing is clearly marked otherwise.

compare.title: School bus lights
rows: Stop at least 20 feet away until they turn off

summary: Michigan's Basic Speed Law requires a careful and prudent speed that lets you stop within the clear distance ahead, never faster than the posted limit. When no limit is posted, standard limits apply, from mobile home parks and subdivisions up to freeways. Freeways also have a minimum speed, and trucks and school buses have lower top speeds.

Pass only when you can see the left lane clearly and have enough distance. Do not pass near intersections, railroad crossings, bridges, or tunnels, on hills or curves, or where a solid yellow line is on your side. Return to your lane well before oncoming traffic, and when someone passes you, do not speed up.

Passing on the right is allowed only in certain cases and never on the shoulder. When parking, turn off the engine, set the parking brake, and turn your wheels so the car cannot roll into traffic. Keep the distances from hydrants, crosswalks, signs, signals, and railroad tracks shown below.

concepts.definition: Unless posted: 15 mph in mobile home parks, 25 mph in platted subdivisions and condo complexes, 55 mph on other roads, and 70 mph maximum, 55 mph minimum on freeways.
concepts.tip: 15, 25, 55, 70: know where each applies.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: On freeways they are limited to 65 mph, or 55 mph where the freeway limit is below 70 mph.
concepts.tip: Expect heavy vehicles to be slower.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: Do not pass within 100 feet of an intersection or railroad crossing, when your view is blocked within 100 feet of a bridge or tunnel, or on a hill or curve where you cannot see far enough ahead.
concepts.tip: 100 feet: intersections, rail crossings, bridges.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: Return to your lane before you are within 200 feet of an oncoming vehicle, and only when you can see the whole passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.
concepts.tip: 200 feet from oncoming traffic.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: Downhill with a curb, turn wheels toward the curb; uphill, away from it. With no curb, turn them so the car will not roll into traffic. Always set the parking brake.
concepts.tip: Downhill: toward the curb.

concepts.definition: Not within 15 feet of a hydrant, 20 feet of a marked crosswalk, 30 feet of a stop sign or signal, or 50 feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing, and not more than 12 inches from the curb.
concepts.tip: 15 hydrant, 20 crosswalk, 30 sign, 50 rail.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

points: Unless posted: 25 mph in subdivisions, 55 mph on other roads, 70 mph on freeways.
Freeways have a 55 mph minimum unless posted otherwise.
Do not pass within 100 feet of an intersection or railroad crossing.
You may pass a bicyclist in a no-passing zone if it is safe.
Never pass on the shoulder.
Never park within 500 feet of a fire or crash.

compare.title: Parking distances to remember
rows: A stop sign, traffic light, or flashing beacon
The nearest rail of a railroad crossing
A fire station driveway, same side
A fire station driveway, other side (when marked)

summary: Safe driving starts with space and time. Keep a following distance of at least three to four seconds and add more at higher speeds and in bad weather. Look well down the road so you can spot problems early instead of reacting at the last second.

Weather and darkness change how you drive. Roads are most slippery when rain first begins, fog calls for low beams and a slow speed, and bridges freeze before the road. At night, use headlights from a half hour after sunset and dim your high beams for oncoming drivers. If you skid, ease off the accelerator and steer where you want to go.

Share the road with care. Large trucks need far more distance to stop and have blind spots, so never cut in front of them. Give bicyclists plenty of room when passing, never share a lane with a motorcycle, and slow down near horse-drawn buggies. Deer are most active at dawn and dusk; if a crash cannot be avoided, brake firmly and stay in your lane.

concepts.definition: Keep at least 3 to 4 seconds behind the vehicle ahead, counting from when it passes a fixed point. Increase to 6 seconds or more at higher speeds or in poor conditions.
concepts.tip: Count one-thousand one, two, three.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: Michigan law requires at least 3 feet between your vehicle and a bicyclist when passing. You may pass a bicyclist in a no-passing zone if it is safe.
concepts.tip: Three feet, every time.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: Watch most at dawn and dusk, especially in fall and spring. If a crash cannot be avoided, do not veer: brake firmly, hold the wheel with both hands, and stay in your lane.
concepts.tip: Don't veer for deer.

concepts.definition: Use headlights from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise and when you cannot see clearly at 500 feet. Do not use high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle.
concepts.tip: Dim within 500 feet.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: In a skid, take your foot off the accelerator and steer where you want to go. With anti-lock brakes, press hard and hold; without them, brake just short of locking the wheels.
concepts.tip: Off the gas, eyes and wheels where you want to go.

concepts.definition: At 55 mph a car can stop in about 130 feet, but a commercial truck needs about 400 feet. Trucks have large blind spots called no zones.
concepts.tip: If you can't see the driver, the driver can't see you.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: Keep 3 to 4 seconds behind them. It is illegal to drive beside a motorcyclist or pass one in the same lane. Motorcycles of 125cc or more may use freeways.
concepts.tip: Give a motorcycle a full lane.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

points: When rain begins, roads are most slippery for the first half hour.
In fog, use low beams; if you cannot see, pull off and turn on your flashers.
Take a 10-minute break at least every two hours on long trips.
If an oncoming car is in your lane, look for an escape to the right.
If your car breaks down, pull far off, turn on flashers, and stay buckled inside.
Follow a horse-drawn buggy at 15 to 20 mph, at least 20 feet back.

summary: Michigan teens under 18 earn a license through Graduated Driver Licensing. They complete two segments of driver education and move through three license levels, gaining privileges as they gain experience. Graduated licensing ends at age 18.

The Level 1 Learner's License allows driving only with a licensed parent, guardian, or designated adult who is at least 21 and sits in the front seat. Before the driving skills test, a teen must log supervised hours, including night driving, and hold the Level 1 license for a set time. The Level 2 Intermediate License adds limits on late-night driving and on young passengers, with exceptions for work and authorized activities.

Adults who have never been licensed get a temporary instruction permit after passing the vision, knowledge, and road sign tests, then practice with a licensed adult before the skills test. All new drivers are on probation for at least three years, and Kelsey's Law bars Level 1 and Level 2 drivers from non-emergency phone calls.

concepts.definition: Driver education can start at 14 years, 8 months with a parent's permission. It includes classroom time, behind-the-wheel time, and observation, and ends with a state exam needing 70 percent.
concepts.tip: Segment 1 comes before any license.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: At least 14 years, 9 months, with Segment 1 done. Drive only with a licensed parent, guardian, or designated adult 21 or older in the front seat.
concepts.tip: Level 1: never drive alone.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: At least 15, Segment 2 done, 50 logged hours including 10 at night, and the Level 1 license held at least six months.
concepts.tip: 50 hours, 10 at night, 6 months.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: At least 16 with Level 1 held 6 months. No driving 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. and no more than one passenger under 21, unless an exception applies.
concepts.tip: Level 2: home by 10, one young passenger.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: At least 17, Level 2 held 6 months, and 12 consecutive months without a moving violation, at-fault crash, suspension, or GDL violation.
concepts.tip: Level 3 is earned with a clean year.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: For new adult drivers and some others. Valid 180 days. Practice at least 30 days with a licensed adult before the driving skills test.
concepts.tip: TIP: 180 days valid, 30 days practice.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

points: Segment 2 needs a 30-hour log with 2 hours at night and Level 1 held three months.
A license for a driver under 21 expires on the 21st birthday.
New drivers are on probation for at least three years.
Under Kelsey's Law, Level 1 and 2 drivers may use a phone only for emergencies.
Level 2 limits do not apply when driving to or from work.

compare.title: The three GDL levels
rows: Only with a licensed parent, guardian, or designated adult 21+
No driving 10 p.m. to 5 a.m.; one passenger under 21 (with exceptions)

summary: Alcohol affects judgment and reaction time, and the effect is the same whether you drink beer, wine, or liquor. A standard can of beer, glass of wine, and shot of whiskey hold the same amount of alcohol. Coffee, cold showers, and fresh air do not help; only time sobers you up. Plan a designated driver before you drink.

Michigan sets clear limits. At the adult limit a driver is operating while intoxicated, a much higher level brings tougher high-BAC penalties, and drivers under 21 may have no alcohol in their body at all. Under implied consent, every licensed driver has already agreed to a chemical test, and refusing leads to a suspension. Driving while impaired by marijuana carries the same penalties as alcohol.

Distraction and safety equipment are covered by law too. Michigan's hands-free law bans holding or manually using a phone while driving, except to report an emergency. Everyone in the front seat and all passengers under 16 must buckle up, and young children ride in a car seat or booster.
Points are added to your driving record when you are convicted of a moving violation. They stay for two years, and too many points within that time can lead to a driver reexamination.

concepts.definition: A BAC of 0.08 or more is operating while intoxicated (OWI). A BAC of 0.17 or more brings enhanced high-BAC penalties. Drivers under 21 may have no bodily alcohol content.
concepts.tip: 0.08 OWI, 0.17 super drunk, under 21 zero.

source.org: Michigan State Police (OHSP), Michigan impaired driving law

concepts.definition: By applying for or renewing a license, you agree to a chemical test. Refusing results in a license suspension and 6 points.
concepts.tip: Refusing the test costs your license.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: Since June 30, 2023, drivers may not hold or manually use a phone while driving, including calls, texts, and video. Voice mode after a single tap and emergency calls are allowed.
concepts.tip: Phone down, hands on the wheel.

source.org: Michigan Vehicle Code, MCL 257.602b (hands-free law)

concepts.definition: Everyone in the front seat and all passengers under 16 must buckle up. Children ride in a car seat or booster until age 8 or 4 feet 9 inches tall.
concepts.tip: Under 8 or under 4'9": car seat or booster.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: Points are posted only after a conviction and stay on your record for two years from the conviction date.
concepts.tip: Points last two years.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: 6 points: OWI, refusing a chemical test, reckless driving. 4 points: drag racing, under 21 with any alcohol, 16+ mph over. 3 points: careless driving, 11 to 15 mph over. 2 points: 6 to 10 mph over, open container.
concepts.tip: Bigger danger, more points.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

concepts.definition: In work zones: 3 points for 10 mph or less over, 4 points for more than 10 up to 15 over, and 5 points for more than 15 over.
concepts.tip: Work zones have their own, higher scale.

source.org: Michigan Department of State, What Every Driver Must Know

points: Only time sobers you up.
Drivers under 21 may not have any alcohol in their body.
Refusing a chemical test brings a suspension and 6 points.
12 or more points within two years can lead to a driver reexamination.
An impaired driving conviction stays on your record permanently.
Children under 4 ride in a rear seat when the vehicle has one.

compare.title: Speeding points: general vs. work zone
